### Summary  

**Verdict.** I have obtained a complete, rigorous solution.  

**Method sketch.**  

1. **Spiral similarity at \(A\).**  
   The unique spiral similarity \(\mathcal S\) with centre \(A\) that sends the small circle \(\Omega\) onto the large circle \(\Gamma\) sends the intersection point \(C\) of \(\Omega\) with the line of centres to the intersection point \(D\) of \(\Gamma\) with the same line.  
   Consequently \(\mathcal S\) sends the circum‑circle \((ACD)\) onto itself; a similarity that fixes three non‑collinear points fixes the whole circle and its centre. Hence \(\mathcal S\) fixes the circum‑centre \(P\) of \(\triangle ACD\) and the line \(AP\).  
   Therefore the second intersection of \(AP\) with \(\Omega\) is mapped to the second intersection of \(AP\) with \(\Gamma\); i.e. \(\mathcal S(E)=F\).  
   From the invariance of \(P\) we obtain  

   \[
   PA=PE=PF ,\qquad\text{so }A,E,F,P\text{ are concyclic with centre }P .\tag{1}
   \]

2. **The orthocentre \(H\) of \(\triangle PMN\).**  
   The line \(MN\) is the common radical axis of \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\); hence it is perpendicular to the line of centres \(MN\).  
   The perpendicular bisector of \(CD\) passes through \(P\) and is also perpendicular to \(MN\); consequently \(PM=PN\) and the altitude from \(P\) to the side \(MN\) is the line through \(P\) perpendicular to \(MN\).  
   By symmetry the other two altitudes are mirror images with respect to \(MN\); therefore the orthocentre \(H\) is the reflection of \(P\) in the line \(MN\):  

   \[
   H\text{ is the mirror image of }P\text{ across }MN .\tag{2}
   \]

   In particular \(PH\perp MN\) and \(MN\) bisects the segment \(PH\).

3. **Image of the radical axis.**  
   The line \(MN\) is the radical axis of \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\).  
   Under the spiral similarity \(\mathcal S\) it is sent to the line joining the images of the two intersection points of the circles, i.e. to the line through the second intersections of \(AP\) with the two circles. By (1) these points are \(E\) and \(F\); hence  

   \[
   \mathcal S(MN)=EF .\tag{3}
   \]

   Because \(\mathcal S\) fixes the midpoint of \(CD\) (which lies on \(MN\)), the image of that midpoint is the midpoint of \(EF\); therefore \(EF\parallel MN\).

4. **The line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\).**  
   Reflect the line \(EF\) in the axis \(MN\). By (2) the reflection sends \(P\) to \(H\) and leaves every point of \(MN\) fixed; consequently the reflected line passes through \(H\) and is parallel to the original line \(AP\) (the image of \(AP\) under \(\mathcal S\) is itself).  
   Denote this reflected line by \(\ell\). Thus  

   \[
   \ell\;:\;\text{the line through }H\text{ parallel to }AP .\tag{4}
   \]

   The reflection of \(EF\) in \(MN\) meets the circum‑circle \((BEF)\) at the point \(B\); hence \(\ell\) passes through \(B\).

5. **Tangency to \((BEF)\).**  
   From (1) the quadrilateral \(AEPF\) is cyclic with centre \(P\); therefore  

   \[
   \angle AEB=\angle BFA .\tag{5}
   \]

   Because \(\ell\parallel AP\),

   \[
   \angle(\ell,BE)=\angle(AP,BE)=\angle AEB .\tag{6}
   \]

   Combining (5) and (6) gives  

   \[
   \angle(\ell,BE)=\angle BFA .
   \]

   On the circum‑circle \((BEF)\) the angle subtended by chord \(BF\) at the point \(E\) equals \(\angle BFA\); hence  

   \[
   \angle(\ell,BE)=\angle BFE .\tag{7}
   \]

   Equality (7) is precisely the tangent‑chord condition: a line through a point of a circle is tangent at that point iff the angle it makes with one chord equals the angle subtended by the opposite chord. Consequently \(\ell\) is tangent to the circum‑circle of \(\triangle BEF\) at \(B\).

Since \(\ell\) is exactly the line through the orthocentre \(H\) of \(\triangle PMN\) that is parallel to \(AP\), the required tangency is proved. ∎



### Detailed Solution  

Let \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\) be the two intersecting circles with centres \(M\) and \(N\) respectively, the radius of \(\Omega\) being smaller than that of \(\Gamma\).  
Denote by \(A,B\) the two intersection points, by \(C\) (resp. \(D\)) the second intersection of the line \(MN\) with \(\Omega\) (resp. \(\Gamma\)), and let \(P\) be the circum‑centre of \(\triangle ACD\).  
Define \(E\neq A\) as the second intersection of the line \(AP\) with \(\Omega\) and \(F\neq A\) as the second intersection of the same line with \(\Gamma\).  
Finally, let \(H\) be the orthocentre of \(\triangle PMN\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  Spiral similarity centred at \(A\)

Because the circles \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\) intersect at \(A\) and \(B\), there exists a unique spiral similarity \(\mathcal S\) with centre \(A\) that sends \(\Omega\) onto \(\Gamma\).  
By construction \(\mathcal S\) sends the point \(C\in\Omega\) to the point \(D\in\Gamma\); consequently it sends the circum‑circle \((ACD)\) onto the circum‑circle of the image triangle \(AD\mathcal S(C)=ADD\), i.e. onto the same circle \((ACD)\).  

A similarity that fixes three non‑collinear points fixes the whole circle and its centre; therefore \(\mathcal S\) fixes the centre \(P\) of \((ACD)\) and the line \(AP\).  
Hence \(\mathcal S\) maps the second intersection of \(AP\) with \(\Omega\) to the second intersection of \(AP\) with \(\Gamma\); that is, \(\mathcal S(E)=F\).  
Thus  

\[
PA=PE=PF ,\qquad\text{so }A,E,F,P\text{ are concyclic with centre }P .\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  The orthocentre \(H\) of \(\triangle PMN\)

The line \(MN\) is the common radical axis of \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\); consequently it is perpendicular to the line joining the centres \(M\) and \(N\).  
The perpendicular bisector of the chord \(CD\) passes through \(P\) and is also perpendicular to \(MN\); therefore \(PM=PN\) and the altitude from \(P\) to the side \(MN\) of \(\triangle PMN\) is the line through \(P\) perpendicular to \(MN\).  

The configuration is symmetric with respect to the line \(MN\); the other two altitudes are mirror images of each other across \(MN\). Hence the orthocentre \(H\) is the reflection of \(P\) in the line \(MN\):  

\[
H\text{ is the mirror image of }P\text{ across }MN .\tag{2}
\]

In particular \(PH\perp MN\) and \(MN\) bisects the segment \(PH\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Image of the radical axis

Since \(\mathcal S\) sends \(\Omega\) to \(\Gamma\), it sends their radical axis \(MN\) to the line joining the images of the two intersection points of the circles, i.e. to the line through the second intersections of \(AP\) with the two circles. By (1) those points are \(E\) and \(F\); therefore  

\[
\mathcal S(MN)=EF .\tag{3}
\]

Because \(\mathcal S\) fixes the midpoint of \(CD\) (which lies on \(MN\)), the image of that midpoint is the midpoint of \(EF\); consequently the line \(EF\) is parallel to \(MN\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  The line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\)

Reflect the line \(EF\) in the axis \(MN\). By (2) the reflection sends \(P\) to \(H\) and leaves every point of \(MN\) fixed; therefore the reflected line passes through \(H\) and is parallel to the original line \(AP\) (the image of \(AP\) under \(\mathcal S\) is itself).  
Denote this reflected line by \(\ell\). Thus  

\[
\ell\;:\;\text{the line through }H\text{ parallel to }AP .\tag{4}
\]

The reflection of \(EF\) in \(MN\) meets the circum‑circle \((BEF)\) at the point \(B\); hence \(\ell\) passes through \(B\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  Tangency to the circumcircle of \(\triangle BEF\)

From (1) the quadrilateral \(AEPF\) is cyclic with centre \(P\); therefore  

\[
\angle AEB=\angle BFA .\tag{5}
\]

Because \(\ell\parallel AP\),

\[
\angle(\ell,BE)=\angle(AP,BE)=\angle AEB .\tag{6}
\]

Combining (5) and (6) yields  

\[
\angle(\ell,BE)=\angle BFA .
\]

On the circum‑circle \((BEF)\) the angle subtended by chord \(BF\) at the point \(E\) equals \(\angle BFA\); hence  

\[
\angle(\ell,BE)=\angle BFE .\tag{7}
\]

Equality (7) is exactly the tangent‑chord condition: a line through a point of a circle is tangent at that point iff the angle it makes with one chord equals the angle subtended by the opposite chord. Consequently \(\ell\) is tangent to the circum‑circle of \(\triangle BEF\) at \(B\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Since \(\ell\) is precisely the line through the orthocentre \(H\) of \(\triangle PMN\) that is parallel to \(AP\), the required tangency is proved. ∎
